# Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the liver > Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/as0Qth)

---

## Summary

Metabolic dysfunction-associated <u>steatotic</u> <u>liver</u> disease (MASLD) is the accumulation of excess fat in <u>hepatocytes</u> in individuals with at least one cardiometabolic <u>risk factor</u> (e.g., <u>hypertension</u>, <u>impaired glucose tolerance</u>) in the absence of an alternative cause (e.g., <u>heavy alcohol use</u>, <u>drug-induced liver injury</u>). MASLD was previously known as nonalcoholic <u>fatty liver</u> disease. It is highly prevalent in patients with <u>type 2 diabetes mellitus</u> (<u>T2DM</u>), <u>obesity</u>, and/or <u>metabolic syndrome</u>. MASLD is usually asymptomatic and is a diagnosis of exclusion. Diagnostic findings may include <u>hepatic steatosis</u> on imaging and <u>elevated transaminases</u>. Patients with MASLD should be assessed for advanced <u>liver fibrosis</u> using a combination of laboratory-based noninvasive testing, such as the <u>FIB-4</u>, and <u>vibration-controlled transient elastography</u>. <u>Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis</u> (<u>MASH</u>) is a subtype of MASLD characterized by chronic <u>hepatocyte</u> inflammation and damage due to lipid accumulation and is associated with a higher risk of progression to <u>liver fibrosis</u> and <u>cirrhosis</u>. <u>MASH</u> was previously known as <u>nonalcoholic steatohepatitis</u> (<u>NASH</u>). <u>Biopsy</u> may be indicated if there is diagnostic uncertainty. Management focuses on the prevention and treatment of associated metabolic conditions.

---

## Definitions

The nomenclature for <u>steatotic</u> <u>liver</u> disease was updated by international <u>liver</u> disease societies in June 2023.  [[1]](/library/4NW3YN0)




* Metabolic dysfunction-associated <u>steatotic</u> <u>liver</u> disease (MASLD) [[1]](/library/4NW3YN0)

* A type of <u>steatotic</u> <u>liver</u> disease that occurs in individuals with ≥ 1 <u>criterion for metabolic syndrome</u> in the absence of an alternative cause (e.g., <u>heavy alcohol use</u>)

* Previously referred to as nonalcoholic <u>fatty liver</u> disease (NAFLD)

* Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (<u>MASH</u>) [[1]](/library/4NW3YN0)

* A subtype of MASLD characterized by chronic hepatocellular inflammation and damage

* Previously referred to as <u>nonalcoholic steatohepatitis</u> (<u>NASH</u>)

---

## Etiology

MASLD is a <u>multifactorial disease</u> with metabolic and genetic components. [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)




* Cardiometabolic <u>risk factors</u>: any <u>criterion for metabolic syndrome</u> [[4]](/library/7fW4nk0)

* <u>Central obesity</u>

* <u>Prediabetes</u> or <u>T2DM</u>

* <u>Hypertension</u> ≥ 130/85 mm Hg or taking <u>antihypertensives</u>

* <u>Hypertriglyceridemia</u>, low <u>HDL cholesterol</u> , or taking <u>lipid-lowering drugs</u>

* Genetic factors: Individuals with a <u>first-degree relative</u> with <u>MASH</u>-related <u>cirrhosis</u> are at increased risk. [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)

---

## Pathophysiology

* MASLD; : excess energy supply → <u>insulin resistance</u> →;  ↑ circulating dietary sugars and free <u>fatty acids</u> → ↑ hepatic free <u>fatty acids</u> → ↑ <u>triglyceride synthesis</u> → <u>hepatic steatosis</u> [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)

* <u>MASH</u> <u>cirrhosis</u>; : oxidative <u>stress</u>, <u>endoplasmic reticulum</u> <u>stress</u>, and <u>inflammasome</u> activation → inflammation and <u>hepatocyte</u> <u>stress</u> and/or <u>death</u> → fibrogenesis → <u>cirrhosis</u> [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)

---

## Clinical features

* Often asymptomatic

* <u>MASH</u> can manifest with signs of advanced <u>liver</u> disease, e.g.: 

* <u>Hepatomegaly</u>, <u>splenomegaly</u>

* <u>Clinical features of cirrhosis</u>

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)[[3]](/library/rfWfnk0)[[4]](/library/7fW4nk0)[[5]](/library/XiV9J80)




Suspect MASLD in patients with <u>risk factors for MASLD</u>, incidental <u>hepatic steatosis</u> on imaging, and/or <u>idiopathic</u> elevation of <u>transaminases</u> for ≥ 6 months.




* MASLD is diagnosed in patients who meet all of the following criteria: [[1]](/library/4NW3YN0) 

* ≥ 1 <u>criterion for metabolic syndrome</u>

* <u>Hepatic steatosis</u> on imaging or <u>biopsy</u>

* Exclusion of alternative causes of <u>hepatic steatosis</u> based on <u>patient history</u> (e.g., current or prior <u>heavy alcohol use</u>) and <u>laboratory studies</u> ± imaging

* Perform <u>noninvasive evaluation for liver fibrosis</u> (i.e., with <u>FIB-4 score</u> ± imaging) in patients with known or suspected MASLD.

* Consider referral for <u>liver biopsy</u> if the diagnosis remains uncertain or <u>MASH</u> is suspected.





> [!TIP]
> It is only possible to distinguish MASLD from <u>alcohol-associated fatty liver</u> disease using <u>patient history</u>.




### Initial studies




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[4]](/library/7fW4nk0)




* <u>Liver chemistries</u>

* <u>Transaminases</u>

* Normal or ↑ <u>AST</u> and/or <u>ALT</u>

* <u>AST/ALT ratio</u> usually < 1

* <u>AST/ALT ratio</u> of > 1 may indicate progression to <u>cirrhosis</u>.

* Normal or ↓ serum <u>albumin</u>

* <u>CBC</u>: normal or ↓ <u>platelet count</u>

* Tests to rule out alternative diagnoses

* All patients: <u>serology</u> for <u>hepatitis B</u> and <u>hepatitis C</u>

* Additional studies based on clinical suspicion, e.g.: [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)

* <u>Serology</u> for <u>type 1 autoimmune hepatitis</u>

* <u>Tissue transglutaminase IgA</u> for <u>celiac disease</u>

* Serum <u>ferritin</u> and <u>transferrin saturation</u> for <u>iron overload disorders</u>

* Testing for <u>alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency</u>

* Serum <u>ceruloplasmin</u> to screen for <u>Wilson disease</u>





> [!NOTE]
> There is often more ALT than <u>AST</u> (<u>AST/ALT ratio</u> < 1) when Lipids infiltrate the Liver.




#### Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> [[6]](/library/FTWgsk0)




* May be used to confirm <u>hepatic steatosis</u> and/or exclude alternative diagnoses  [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)

* Often nondiagnostic in patients with mild <u>steatosis</u>

* Supportive finding: ↑ <u>liver</u> <u>echogenicity</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Transaminase</u> levels and abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> findings can be normal even in patients with advanced <u>MASH</u> and/or <u>liver fibrosis</u> and therefore should not be used to exclude advanced <u>liver</u> disease. [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)




### Noninvasive evaluation for liver fibrosis [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)[[3]](/library/rfWfnk0)[[4]](/library/7fW4nk0)[[5]](/library/XiV9J80)




#### Indications for <u>noninvasive evaluation for liver fibrosis</u>




* Known MASLD

* <u>Prediabetes</u> or <u>T2DM</u> [[7]](/library/B3Vzk80)

* ≥ 2 <u>criteria for metabolic syndrome</u>  [[3]](/library/rfWfnk0)

* <u>First-degree relative</u> with <u>MASH</u>-related <u>cirrhosis</u>

* Incidental finding of <u>hepatic steatosis</u> on imaging

* <u>Idiopathic</u> <u>elevated transaminases</u> for ≥ 6 months





#### <u>Serology</u>




* <u>FIB-4</u>: preferred   [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)

* Low-risk score (i.e., < 1.3 in adults 35–65 years or < 2.0 in adults ≥ 65 years) [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)[[8]](/library/GudBs70)

* <u>Prediabetes</u>, <u>T2DM</u>, and/or ≥ 2 <u>criteria for metabolic syndrome</u>: Repeat <u>FIB-4</u> score every 1–2 years. [[7]](/library/B3Vzk80)

* All others: Repeat <u>FIB-4</u> score every 2–3 years.

* Indeterminate score: Obtain imaging for <u>liver</u> stiffness measurement, if available; consider referral to hepatology.  [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)[[3]](/library/rfWfnk0)

* High-risk score (i.e., > 2.67): Refer to hepatology for advanced diagnostics. [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)[[8]](/library/GudBs70)

* <u>NAFLD score</u>

* <u>APRI score</u>





#### Imaging tests




Imaging tests are used for <u>liver</u> stiffness measurement.




* <u>Vibration-controlled transient elastography</u> (<u>VCTE</u>): best initial test for patients with an indeterminate or high risk on noninvasive testing [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)[[4]](/library/7fW4nk0)

* Low risk (< 8.0 kPA): Continue with <u>FIB-4</u> screening every 1–3 years.

* Indeterminate risk (8.0–12 kPA) or high risk (> 12.0 kPA): Refer to hepatology.

* <u>MR elastography</u>: Consider if there is diagnostic uncertainty after <u>VCTE</u>.  [[3]](/library/rfWfnk0)

#### <u>Liver biopsy</u> [[3]](/library/rfWfnk0)[[4]](/library/7fW4nk0)




* Indications 

* Diagnostic uncertainty after noninvasive testing and imaging

* Suspicion of <u>MASH</u> (<u>gold standard</u>)

* Supportive findings for MASLD: hepatocellular lipid accumulation, mostly macrovesicular

* Additional findings in <u>MASH</u>

* <u>Necrosis</u> and ballooning degeneration

* Inflammatory infiltrates with scattered <u>lymphocytes</u>, <u>neutrophils</u>, and <u>Kupffer cells</u>

* <u>Steatosis</u>





> [!TIP]
> The diagnosis of <u>MASH</u> requires histological evidence of <u>steatohepatitis</u>. Noninvasive testing can estimate <u>fibrosis</u> stage but cannot confirm <u>MASH</u>. [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)

## Management

### General principles




* Management is focused on the prevention and treatment of associated metabolic conditions.

* Provide <u>multidisciplinary care</u> (e.g., involve the primary care physician, endocrinologist, hepatologist, and dietitian).

* Patients previously classified as low risk for <u>liver fibrosis</u>: Continue ongoing periodic <u>noninvasive evaluation for liver fibrosis</u> based on <u>risk factors</u>.

* Refer to hepatology for:

* Further assessment in patients with indeterminate or high-risk noninvasive test results

* Pharmacological management to reduce <u>hepatic steatosis</u>

* Management of advanced <u>liver fibrosis</u> or <u>cirrhosis</u>





### Nonpharmacological management [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)[[3]](/library/rfWfnk0)[[4]](/library/7fW4nk0)[[9]](/library/hydcUs0)




* Lifestyle changes

* Healthy diet (e.g., <u>Mediterranean diet</u>)

* Regular exercise

* Avoidance of <u>alcohol</u>

* Weight loss for patients with <u>overweight</u>

* Management of associated metabolic conditions

* <u>Management of diabetes mellitus</u>

* <u>Management of obesity</u>

* <u>Management of hypertension</u>

* <u>Management of ASCVD</u>

* <u>Management of malnutrition in adults</u>





### Pharmacological management [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)[[3]](/library/rfWfnk0)




Consider the following medications in consultation with a specialist (e.g., hepatologist) to achieve weight loss goals and/or reduce <u>hepatic steatosis</u> and/or <u>steatohepatitis</u>:




* MASLD

* <u>SGLT-2 inhibitor</u> (e.g., <u>dapagliflozin</u> or <u>empagliflozin</u>) for patients with <u>T2DM</u> [[10]](/library/RgWlEk0)[[11]](/library/3gWSEk0)

* <u>Tirzepatide</u> for patients with <u>T2DM</u> or <u>obesity</u> [[12]](/library/hgWcEk0)

* <u>MASH</u>

* All patients without <u>cirrhosis</u>: vitamin E (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[9]](/library/hydcUs0)

* Patients with moderate to advanced <u>fibrosis</u> (stages F2-F3)

* <u>GLP-1 receptor agonist</u> (e.g., <u>semaglutide</u> DOSAGE) [[13]](/library/6hVjU80)

* OR <u>resmetirom</u> DOSAGE [[14]](/library/JhVsU80)

* Patients with concomitant TD2M: <u>pioglitazone</u> [[2]](/library/IfWYnk0)





> [!TIP]
> There are currently no <u>FDA</u>-approved medications for the <u>treatment of MASLD</u> without <u>fibrosis</u>. <u>Semaglutide</u> or <u>resmetirom</u> are approved for <u>MASH</u> with moderate to advanced <u>fibrosis</u>. [[13]](/library/6hVjU80)[[14]](/library/JhVsU80)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Alcohol-associated liver disease</u>

* <u>Drug-induced liver injury</u> due to: 

* <u>Amiodarone</u>

* <u>Methotrexate</u>

* <u>Tamoxifen</u>

* <u>Valproate</u>

* <u>Antiretroviral drugs</u>

* <u>Corticosteroids</u>

* Viral <u>hepatitis</u>

* <u>Hepatitis C</u>

* <u>Hepatitis B</u>

* Inherited or autoimmune disorders

* <u>Hemochromatosis</u>

* <u>Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency</u>

* <u>Wilson disease</u>

* <u>Autoimmune hepatitis</u>

* <u>Reye syndrome</u>

* <u>Pregnancy</u>-related conditions

* <u>HELLP syndrome</u>

* <u>Acute fatty liver of pregnancy</u>

* Nutrition-related conditions

* <u>Malnutrition</u>

* Acute weight loss (e.g., from <u>metabolic surgery</u> or <u>starvation</u>)

* <u>Celiac disease</u>

* <u>Parenteral nutrition</u>

* See also “<u>Causes of elevated transaminases</u>.”




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Complications

* Advanced <u>liver fibrosis</u>, <u>cirrhosis</u>

* <u>Hepatocellular carcinoma</u>




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
